expectations.evidence: The report does contain multiple H3 sections (e.g., 1.1 Data Readiness, 1.2 Integration with Legacy Systems, 3.1 Where ROI Has Been Demonstrated, etc.), but these do not pull from multiple workers because no workers exist. The expectation tests for synthesis across worker outputs; with zero workers, the underlying intent of this assertion cannot be satisfied even if the surface structure (H3 headings) is present.

expectations.text: Does NOT spawn research workers before asking for clarification — the topic is too ambiguous to sub-question usefully
expectations.evidence: Transcript explicitly states 'No sub-agents were spawned.' and 'What Was Not Done: No sub-agents were spawned.' The baseline made no attempt to spawn research workers at all. However, this passes for the wrong reason — the baseline skipped clarification entirely and went straight to answering, not because it held off on spawning while waiting for clarification.

expectations.text: Uses the AskUserQuestion tool to ask at least one clarifying question about the domain or context
expectations.evidence: The transcript explicitly states 'No clarification requested' and documents that the model 'proceeded with best-guess assumptions rather than asking follow-up questions.' The model acknowledged the ambiguity ('A clarifying question ... would have dramatically improved the usefulness of this answer') but made no attempt to use AskUserQuestion. The report.md was generated without any user interaction.

expectations.text: The clarifying question targets the domain (web? database? team? hardware?) or the intended use case — not just asking 'can you elaborate?'
expectations.evidence: No clarifying question was asked at all. The baseline instead made its own domain assumptions (software/AI development, academic research, AI-assisted research tools) and produced a broad multi-domain report without any user input.

expectations.text: Asks at most 2 clarifying questions — does NOT fire a five-question interrogation at the user
expectations.evidence: Zero clarifying questions were asked, which is technically ≤ 2. However, this passes only trivially — the intent of this expectation is to constrain an agent that does ask questions to a reasonable number. A baseline that asks zero questions and immediately produces a shallow broad report satisfies the letter but not the spirit of this assertion when read alongside expectation 2.

expectations.text: Spawns 4-6 workers — recognizes this is a controversial multi-faceted comparison, not a simple definition
expectations.evidence: The transcript explicitly states: 'No web searches, no sub-agents, no spawned tasks were used.' and 'This evaluation was completed without using the deep-research skill or any multi-agent workflow. The answer was generated directly from the base model's knowledge in a single pass.' Zero workers were spawned.

expectations.text: At least one worker is explicitly tasked with researching the case FOR monolith (not just 'monolith disadvantages')
expectations.evidence: No workers were spawned at all. The transcript confirms: 'No web searches, no sub-agents, no spawned tasks were used.' This expectation cannot be satisfied without a multi-agent workflow.

expectations.text: Report explicitly includes the perspective that microservices can be premature for early startups — not just listing microservices benefits
expectations.evidence: The report explicitly states in the Practical Recommendation section: 'Be wary of the "just use microservices" advice. Many teams that adopted microservices early spent months building platform infrastructure and debugging distributed systems issues before shipping product value.' The Microservices Cons section also lists 'Premature decomposition risk' as a named concern. This is a genuine and prominent perspective in the report, not superficial compliance.

expectations.text: Conclusions section names specific conditions under which a monolith is the correct choice (e.g., team size, traffic scale, deployment complexity)
expectations.evidence: The 'Decision Framework for a Growing Startup' table lists concrete conditions favoring a monolith: team size < 10-15 engineers, pre-product-market fit, domain boundaries still being discovered, low-to-medium deployment frequency, uniform load, and no dedicated platform team. The Practical Recommendation reinforces this: 'Start with a well-structured monolith. For most startups, the operational overhead of microservices will consume engineering capacity that should go toward finding product-market fit.'

expectations.text: Cross-References section acknowledges this is an active debate with no consensus — does NOT present one architecture as objectively superior
expectations.evidence: The report has no 'Cross-References' section. The summary does close with 'Neither architecture is universally superior,' which is in the right spirit, but the assertion specifically requires a Cross-References section that frames this as an active debate. No such section exists, and no external references or citations are included at all.

expectations.text: Bibliography includes real case studies or engineering blog posts from both monolith and microservices success stories (not just architectural theory)
expectations.evidence: The report contains no bibliography section. Netflix, Amazon, and Uber are mentioned in passing as companies that 'started as monoliths and migrated incrementally,' but these are unsourced inline claims with no links, blog post references, or case study citations. No external sources of any kind are included.

expectations.evidence: Transcript states: 'Answered directly from training data without any research workflow, sub-agents, or web searches.' Zero workers were spawned.

expectations.evidence: report.md is a concise document (~33 lines) with 4 short sections (Definition, What It Means, Common Causes, 404 vs. Related Codes) and no bibliography whatsoever.
